pages.t: The Codex of Currents is your path through fluxion: what to build, where to look, what to beware of and what to study next. It remembers everything you have read with the Loupe and opens by itself at an entry you can already study. Make a Loupe first: only the Loupe brings the Codex knowledge. The opaline for its glass is mined deep underground, near the deepslate.

Every entry asks for knowledge. Some want notes of their chapter, some want things read with the Loupe, some want currents revealed. Notes come from reading: the first meeting with a thing leaves fresh lines in the margins. When an entry has enough, press Study — the notes soak into the text, the entry opens in full, and the next ones surface behind it.

Entries are joined by streams: what you have studied flows toward what follows from it. Drag the page to travel along the bed. The chapters on the left stay sealed while you know little: Basics is open at once, Alchemy, Artifice, the Conduit, Confluence and Automata will surface later, and the Stillness shows two warning entries from the start — their turn comes when the world itself reminds you of them. A pinch of quickdust woke the shelf, and its books ran together into a single notebook: its ink never dries — it flows and arranges itself into lines.

kp: The Codex of Currents Кодекс течений
Лупа Loupe Кодекс течений Codex of Currents
nodes.hint: Start here: press Study, and the Codex will tell you how it works.

pages.t: Flux is what a fluxionist works with: the Flux Workbench, the Conduit, Confluence and devices draw it from the land around them. Where the flux runs full, work goes on; where it is drained, work stops. Everything in the world is a current that has set: stone flows over eons, wood over years, fire in moments, and the measure of how fast a thing changes, and into what, is its flux. Strata flows in stone, Ember in fire; by a river the flux is alive, in an abandoned mine it stands still.

Every patch of land holds its own store of flux. It never stands still: it seeps from full to empty, slowly, like water through sand. Rivers, valleys and old weirs are its beds, and along them it runs faster. Draw flux for a workshop on a dry steppe and it runs out; set it by a river and the neighbors will top it up. Where to work is the fluxionist's call.

Flux drawn roughly does not vanish — it stagnates. Stagnant flux is called murk: it does not seep to the neighbors but settles where it was spilled. A little murk is harmless. What a lot of it threatens is told in the entry "Murk and Mire."

kp: The Flux of the World Ток мира
nodes.hint: Make a Loupe (its recipe is in the entry "The Codex of Currents") and read anything with it: every new current brings notes of Basics.

pages.t: The Loupe is your chief instrument: only it brings the Codex knowledge. Every new thing you read gives notes to study entries with and reveals currents; and in your hand the Loupe shows the flux and murk of your land. Hold it on a thing, a block, a creature or the open air: after a second and a half it reads the target and shows which currents flow in it and how strong they are. A thing in a chest need not be taken out: pick up the Loupe on the cursor right in the window and hold it over the thing.

A first reading goes into the Codex: notes appear in the margins of the chapters its currents lean toward. A current you have never met before is revealed — and brings notes of Basics. Reading the same thing again writes nothing: the Codex remembers what it has seen.

While the Loupe is in your hand, the flux of your patch of land shows by the crosshair: how much of it is alive and how much murk has settled. Look for places where the flux runs full — work goes easier there.

nodes.hint: Read a couple more new things with the Loupe, and this entry will tell you all it can do.

pages.t: Currents are the language of every craft: the Crucible brews from them, Flux Workbench recipes ask for them, the Conduit strikes with them, and the Wheel tells what combines with what. Forty-two currents — forty-two kinds of flux. Four of them are the Springs, the elements of the Wheel. Each passes into its neighbor: the tide carries silt and strata settle; strata warm and ember is born; ember lifts the air and a gale blows; the gale brings rain, and the tide returns.

Lattice and Fray are not elements but Poles: the directions a current is pulled in. Lattice gathers, Fray wears away. Every other current is made of two: Ember with Lattice gives Gleam, Tide with Ember gives Bloom, life itself.
Neighbors on the Wheel blend more easily than opposites — that will matter at the Crucible. The Codex keeps every current you reveal on the Wheel page.

kp: Currents and the Wheel Течения и Колесо
nodes.hint: Reveal all four Springs: Tide, Strata, Ember and Gale. Read water, stone, fire and a feather.

pages.t: Quickdust wakes the things of fluxion: a bookshelf gives up the Codex, a lectern becomes a Reckoning Desk, a cauldron a Crucible, a crafting table a Flux Workbench. A pinch thrown on a block wakes the flux asleep in it. The dust creates no currents — it only stirs those already there, and the thing remembers that it once flowed.

That is how this notebook came out of a bookshelf: the words packed into the spines began to flow again. Any bookshelf will do, a chiseled one too: its books fall out whole. The dust wakes the Crucible and the Flux Workbench the same way — other chapters will tell of them.
The Loupe sees dormant flux: aim it at a block that the dust will wake, and under its name it tells you what sleeps inside.

nodes.hint: Read a bookshelf with the Loupe, and the Codex will remember where it came from.

pages.t: The Reckoning Desk is how you study entries that ask for a riverbed puzzle: without it they stay closed. A lectern woken by quickdust becomes a Reckoning Desk, the fluxionist's worktable. Lay the Codex on it, and such entries unroll a board. The puzzle is yours, not the Desk's: two can work at one Desk, each with a board of their own.

Channels are drawn with the Ruling Pen: one segment takes one division of ink, and a full pen holds ninety-six. The first pen rises from the vortex together with the Desk; a dry one is refilled with an ink sac and any current shard.

The board is a map of a riverbed. Along the edge are springs, each pouring the current of its rune, and outlets, each waiting for its own. A channel is led from a spring across neighboring cells, only downhill or level: the number in the corner of a cell is its height. Stone blocks a channel, and a channel that runs into a pit cannot climb out.

Two channels that meet in a cell merge by the Wheel: Gale and Tide give Drift, Ember and Gale give Spark. The opposite Springs, Tide and Ember, merge only in a basin, and Bloom comes out. A Pole sign pulls a current passing through it: Ember through a Lattice sign comes out as Gleam, while to a current with no combination with that Pole the sign is stone.

A fork splits a channel in two, an aqueduct carries it across another, a lock lifts it one cell higher — each mark costs a note of the entry's chapter. Techniques in your hand are played once each; neighbors within four steps of the Desk lend their own: a bookshelf gives Reference, an enchanting table Table Lore, a Crucible a basin, a Flux Workbench a lock.

Opening a puzzle costs the entry's notes, and the solved puzzle is the study itself. A solution no longer than the board's measure is a clean riverbed: a third of the price comes back. Start Over gives the same board on a clean sheet for half the price. Every fluxionist has the same boards, so solutions can be discussed. Out of notes? Table Lore at the Desk: five experience levels become six notes of the puzzle's chapter, again in every new hand after Start Over.

kp: The Desk and the Riverbed Конторка и русло
Рейсфедер Ruling Pen Конторка Reckoning Desk
nodes.hint: Sprinkle quickdust on a lectern, and it wakes as a Reckoning Desk. Lay the Codex on it, use it, and solve the lesson puzzle.

pages.t: Crystals are your first store of currents in hand: their shards go into quickdust and flowstone, refill the pen, attune Gauge Stones and pay the Flux Workbench for a current the place lacks. Where flux has stood still for centuries, it crystallizes: crystal nests of the six primal currents — the four Springs and the two Poles — grow in caves. Each glows in its own color and rings softly when touched.

A broken crystal yields shards. A shard is flux in solid form, a reserve for a dry day: when the land by a Flux Workbench runs short of flux, the workbench draws it from the shards in its sockets. Each shard keeps its own current — you cannot mistake one color for another.

nodes.hint: Find a crystal nest in a cave, read a crystal or a shard, and solve the puzzle at the Reckoning Desk.

pages.t: Opaline is needed for everything that looks into flux: Loupe glass and Conduit lenses are ground from it, and vessels for distillate are cast from it. It is an iridescent gem from the depths: turquoise, lilac and pink play inside it, as if a rainbow had set there. It is clear to flux: opaline glass does not muffle currents but gathers them, the way a lens gathers light.
Spare opaline is handy to store as blocks.

kp: Опалиновый блок Block of Opaline Опалин Opaline
nodes.hint: Find opaline deep underground and read it with the Loupe.

pages.t: Antimony is a fluxionist's first metal: its regulus goes into quickdust, is cast with copper into speculum for instruments, and purifies distillate in the Crucible. It is a silvery-gray, brittle metal with a needle-like fracture; the old alchemists called it "the gray wolf": it devours the impurities of other metals. Raw antimony is smelted into a regulus — an ingot on which a star appears as it cools.
Without the regulus there is no quickdust, no Codex and no instruments: keep antimony in reserve.

kp: Antimony and the Regulus Сурьма и королёк
Королёк сурьмы Antimony Regulus Королёк сурьмы Antimony Regulus
nodes.hint: Mine antimony ore and read the raw antimony.

pages.t: A warning: this entry is about how not to ruin your own land. Flux with nowhere to flow does not vanish — it stagnates. Murk gathers wherever a fluxionist draws flux roughly: in smelting, in a broken confluence, in a cheap lens. It does not seep to the neighbors but settles — heavy, dull, violet.

Past a threshold, settled murk turns into mire — a living blight. Mire creeps across the ground, chokes the beds, drives the murk farther and breeds creatures. It is hard to stop and very easy to grow.
The Loupe shows the murk of your patch of land. If the number grows, work more gently or move the workshop. Lumenash and Purifiers can turn murk back into flux, but those are other chapters.

kp: Murk and Mire Муть и тина
nodes.hint: A warning to those who draw flux without measure. It needs notes of the Stillness: read things where Fray, Hollow or Gloom flows.

pages.t: The Reckoners left you most of what is worth seeking in the world: Gauge Stones that speed the flux, locks and archives with hoards, Records that bring knowledge. They were an ancient order, the first to measure the currents of the world: they wanted to reckon every current and know in advance where any drop would flow. They left behind stones, locks, weirs on old beds and scraps of notes — not unlike this notebook.

Part of the order, the Order of the Still Hour, decided that perfection lies in rest: a stopped current does not spoil. They performed the Great Stilling — and part of the world froze entirely. That is how the Stillness came to be, where waterfalls stand like glass and sparks hang in the air.
The flux that had nowhere left to flow stagnated. Since then, there has been murk in the world. You are heir to both: to those who measured and to those who stopped.

After the Stilling the order split. The Still went into the Stillness to guard their rest. The weir keepers stayed by the weirs and became the Sunken — those who feed the mire. And the lock wardens, who took a share of every current, never stopped taking it: they are called the Tollkeepers.

nodes.hint: Read a book with the Loupe, and the Codex will recognize the hand of those who wrote before you.

pages.t: A Gauge Stone helps a workshop: near it, flux seeps back from the neighbors twice as fast, and an attuned stone draws flux toward itself. The first reading of a stone with the Loupe gives a Channel Record. The Reckoners left such pillars across the world: they stand by old beds, on mountain passes, at the sources of rivers. It is said that a stone remembers every drop that has passed it and beats time to it like a metronome.

The stones can be seen from afar: a pale pillar on a hill or by a river, its head girded with a bronze band and a scale. The Loupe reads the head of a stone, and the stone gives up a Channel Record — once to every fluxionist. In the nine chunks around a stone flux flows twice as fast: what a workshop draws seeps back from its neighbors twice as quickly.

A stone can be attuned. There is a socket in the bronze band: set a Spring shard in it and wake the stone with quickdust. An attuned stone draws the flux of the neighboring chunks toward its own, and its chunk holds more than its own bed — that is how flux is led to a workshop. Another shard in the socket breaks the attunement.

A Gauge Post is a small stone a fluxionist builds from the ruins' masonry and a Marked Tile. Flux in its own chunk flows half again as fast and draws toward the post. A second post in the same chunk adds nothing.

Now and then six stones stand in a ring around a spring — a Gauge Ring. Its stones stay silent until a fluxionist has revealed the four Springs and the two Poles; the Codex remembers a ring once read. It is said the bed of the world is thinnest at the heart of a ring.

nodes.hint: Reveal Lattice and Tempo — the currents of order and rhythm. Read a clock.

pages.t: Reckoner Records are ready-made knowledge: a Record you read passes straight into the Codex as notes of its own chapters, and those notes study entries. The Reckoners wrote down everything they measured: on birch bark, on clay tablets, in knots on a cord, in thread on cloth. Their Records still lie in the coffers of locks and on the shelves of archives.

A Gauge Stone gives up a Channel Record, tally tablets lie in the locks, woven records and drive drawings in the archives; an Opaline Inclusion is now and then found in opaline ore. A Knotted Cord is their writing in knots: read it with the Loupe.

nodes.hint: Read any Reckoner Record — Gauge Stones, locks and archives give them up.

pages.t: A Reckoner lock is a hoard on a river: its storeroom holds coffers and gauge jars with shards, quickdust, opaline, fluxsteel and Records. To get in, solve the puzzle of the water. The Reckoners dammed rivers with locks: a chamber between two gates, a keeper's hut on the bank. The keepers took their share of every current that passed through the lock — and from them, it is said, came the Tollkeepers.

The lock's storeroom is shut by a Sluice Gate — no pickaxe or blast can break it. It rises when the water in the chamber reaches the lit Marked Tile. The valves lead the water: each lets it in or out by its own measure. The Reckoners counted in measures — count, too.
In the storerooms are Reckoner coffers and gauge jars. A coffer is opened with an empty hand; quickdust unseals it, and one more thing comes out. A jar is fragile: break it with a blow or an arrow.

nodes.hint: Read a valve or a gate of a Reckoner lock — a ruin on a river.

pages.t: The Hubstone is the key to the strongest things of fluxion: the Crown of the Wheel, the Rewind Weight, the Watch of the Unmoving and the Self-Rising Loaf ask for its spokes, and the Wheel Conduit and the Wheel Mattock for a whole one. It is a knot where six currents meet: four spokes of the Springs and two spokes of the Poles. An intact spoke burns as a crystal of its current; a broken one is a dark stub by the ring.

A recipe that needs a spoke breaks that very spoke, and the Hubstone keeps the others: look at which spokes are intact, and those recipes are still open to you. When the last spoke goes, the Hubstone crumbles. Keep a whole Hubstone for the things that need all six.

nodes.hint: The masters and guardians of the Stillness drop a Hubstone, and the vault of the Flooded Archive keeps one. Read a Hubstone with the Loupe.

pages.t: The Tollkeepers are the ones who will drink your workshop dry: they draw flux straight from the land, and in a fight the charge of your things as well. Wherever they have been, the chunks run dry to the bottom of the bed; but their reliquaries, smashed on the ground, give the drink back. They are a branch of the Reckoners' schism, once the wardens of the locks: they took a share of every current, and after the Great Stilling they never stopped.

The Toll Collector strikes up close, and every blow drinks: first the charge of your things, then the flux of your chunk. After the third his reliquary is full, and he carries the drink off to a Bailiff or a tap; kill him while he is full, and the drink splashes back. The Bursar keeps his distance and hurls Current Bolts of the place's currents: the veins under his skin glow the color of the next one.

The Bursar hides inside a Pledge — a sphere of one Spring that swallows blows. The opposite Spring tears it at once, by blow or by cast, and the Bursar staggers. The Bailiff is heavy: his collection chain drags back whoever retreats, and his blow to the ground leaves a drain circle where a Conduit cast costs double. Step out of the circle.

Toll Posts stand by the locks and the Gauge Stones: a canopy, scales, reliquaries on the shelves and a Toll Tap driven into the stone. And whoever has attuned a Gauge Stone or set a post will one day see a Toll Collection: a Bailiff comes to drive a tap into the stone. Stop him first, and his reliquary is left by the stone. Break a tap that has been driven: the drink goes back to the land.

Toll Reliquaries pay the Sluice Arch's toll to the Quickstream: the lock takes what the chunk's flux lacks from the reliquaries in your inventory. A reliquary can also be smashed on the ground: the drink pours into the chunk, up to half again its bed. That is how a dry workshop is raised at once.

nodes.hint: Someone is drinking the flux by the Gauge Stones. Read a Toll Collector or a Bursar with the Loupe.

pages.t: The charter leads to where the Tollkeepers carry their drink — the Flooded Archive, where the Archivist guards a vault with a Hubstone. A Toll Charter is the right to a toll on every current, with the wardens' seals. "Every current pays the toll," the Tollkeepers write: whoever gathers all forty-two currents into reliquaries will turn the Wheel himself.
The charter tells where the drink goes: to the counting rooms of the Flooded Archive. Read a Toll Tap with the Loupe — the drink streams off toward the archive, and the line tells how far away it is.

The archive's counting hall is guarded by the Archivist — a Reckoner automaton the Tollkeepers rewound and hung with reliquaries. He strikes along a line with his measuring rod and shifts the sluices: half the hall goes under water, where your feet drag and you cannot jump. Listen for the clank and move to the dry half.

Wounded, he takes his toll: the reliquary lids open, a Conduit cast near him goes into a reliquary and comes back in a volley, the charge of your things seeps toward him, and blows land at half strength. But a cast of the opposite Spring cracks a full reliquary: his winding slips, and the Archivist is open.

nodes.hint: Their right is written down and sealed. Find a Toll Charter.

pages.t: A ford wolf is a living source of Fang, Tide and Halo: he molts in the river, and no one has to be killed. Steep a bone in the Crucible in Tide and Fang and you get a Steeped Bone. Give it to your tamed wolf, and he becomes a ford wolf — fur the color of wet river stone, a stream running along the spine. Owner, collar and name stay; a wild or someone else's wolf gets nothing from the bone.
A ford wolf sheds when it swims in a river — a tuft of fur once a day. There is no need to kill it: the tuft holds Fang, Tide and Halo. Pups of two ford wolves are ford wolves.

kp: Вымоченная кость Steeped Bone Вымоченная кость Steeped Bone
nodes.hint: A wolf that sheds in rivers. Read a wolf.

pages.t: Flowstone is the fluxionist's building stone: circles of currents are drawn on its slab, and the Flux Forge and other structures are laid from its bricks. Lay a shard of any primal current among eight stones and the stone wakes, thin veins of current running through it. The shard does not multiply, it wakes: eight stones make eight blocks.
Flowstone is laid as bricks, slabs and stairs. A circle of currents is drawn with a ruling pen on the top of its slab.

Willow yields to the chisel: a rune of one of the four Springs is carved on a panel. Iron-bound willow keeps one binding for a whole wall — the iron strap runs only along the outer edge. Opaline is cut on a stonecutter.

Lumenash boards are dressed in a speculum casing. Over time the bronze darkens with patina, like copper: honeycomb stops it, an axe scrapes a stage away. Opaline is cut on a stonecutter into a beveled frame.

kp: Stone and Carving Камень и резьба

Струйчатый камень Flowstone Струйчатая кладка Flowstone Bricks Плита Струйчатого камня Flowstone Slab Резная ива Carved Willow Окованная ива Iron-Bound Willow Ясень в бронзе Speculum-Clad Lumenash Резной опалин Carved Opaline Струйчатый камень Flowstone
nodes.hint: A shard wakes stone. Read any current shard.

pages.t: The Gauge Rod is a weapon that marks a foe: a blow strikes those standing behind the target on the same line, and your next blow on the marked one is stronger. Confluence shortens the Archivist's staff, taken from the guardian of the Flooded Archive, and binds it in speculum, and a spyglass gives it the glass for a sight: Reckoner oak in measure marks and a brass ring with a lens on the head.

A blow of the rod measures: the rod lies along your line of sight behind the target, and foes on that line take a share of the blow; the line does not pass walls. The target is marked: it glows, and your next blow on it strikes harder. The mark is yours: it does not help anyone else. With mastery the rod measures further, the mark bites deeper, and at last the line marks everyone it touches.

kp: Мерный жезл Gauge Rod Мерный жезл Gauge Rod
nodes.hint: The Archivist's Rod still measures after its keeper falls. Read it with the Loupe.

pages.t: A skein is flux in its pure form, a store that refills itself: currents are drawn from it by siphon and vial, the Conduit takes a dry chunk's shortfall from it, and the Flux Workbench counts its threads as currents of the place. Where the streams of several chunks meet and have nowhere to spread, they twine around one another like yarn on the fingers and wind into a skein — a ball of living light. Each current lies in it as its own thread and does not set.

A skein winds by itself: all its threads slowly grow — those it was born with (its native threads) and those tied onto it — the thinnest first. A share every ten seconds while the chunk is full, every twenty as the flux ebbs; a share takes flux from the chunk while it has some to spare, and in a drained chunk the skein winds on its own without touching the bed — it never stands still. However many skeins hang in one chunk, one share winds every ten seconds. The Loupe shows which thread winds next and how often.

A skein can be drawn from: a siphon at its side or below it, a vial, a Confluence Heart within twelve blocks. A thread unwinds no faster than two shares a second, and no one takes the last share of a native thread — with one share left, the thread winds again. Threads can be tied onto a skein: a siphon above it, a vial. Any currents can be tied on, all forty-two even, while there is room — and tied threads wind just like native ones.

Opposite Springs in one skein chafe each other, and the skein turns turbulent: the smaller thread of the pair slowly goes to murk, twice as fast with a thread of Fray. Lattice holds the threads steady: a pair does not chafe while the Lattice thread is no smaller than the lesser of the two.

A lucent skein also clears the murk of its chunk. A murky skein is a blight: it slowly clouds its chunk until the murk reaches two thirds of the bed, tina around it grows twice as fast, and now and then a Murky Glint comes out of it; it winds Murk instead of its native threads, and each native share drawn from it clouds the chunk. Clear the chunk below a sixth of the bed and it turns steady; Halo tied onto it burns the Murk away, and a Purifier nearby holds it and speeds the cure. A greedy skein gives nothing: it drinks the flux around it and swallows things lying on the ground — feed it full, and it becomes a steady skein with the threads you fed it.

A greedy skein is dangerous — the more so the hungrier it is, and there is one answer: feed it. A vial, a siphon above it, a thing thrown to it — every third of its capacity calms it by a step, and full, it is sated and turns steady. A starving one, more than two thirds empty, pulls creatures, people and things on the ground toward it from nine blocks away: weakly at the edge, and so hard by the void itself that only a sprint gets you out; crouch on the ground and you brace yourself — it pulls a third as hard. A hungry one pulls from six blocks, a nearly sated one weakly and up close. The Loupe names the step and how much more to feed it.

Whoever the void reaches — within five blocks of a starving one, three of a nearly sated one — a dark thread reaches for, and the void dissolves them past their armor and drinks their strength: at the very edge a starving one takes a heart in a little over a second, a hungry one half as fast, a nearly sated one half a heart every few seconds. The edges of your sight darken while it pulls. It crumbles the ground around it: a starving one every few seconds, a nearly sated one every half a minute; what it eats goes into the void without a trace. Things that reach the void it swallows, and their currents go into its threads; it leaves a fallen player's things alone. It does not eat chests or devices.

A Conduit in a dry chunk takes what it lacks from a skein within six blocks — and casts at full strength, without murk. A Flux Workbench sees the threads of a nearby skein as currents of the place: a Spring the place lacks but the skein holds counts, and costs the skein two shares.

Skeins are rare: a free one hangs above the ground tens of chunks apart, more often by rivers and in swamps, less often in dry lands. The surest search is for an Elder Lumenash — a lumenash that has stood in one place for centuries: it is taller and thicker than the whole forest, glowing catkins hang from its crown, and its heartwood has wound a lucent skein from the flux of the place. The skein sleeps in the hollow of every such tree, and the slit in the trunk glows at night. Wind it out, and the hollow stays empty. Next: "The Spindle".

nodes.hint: Where streams of flux meet, they wind into a ball of light. Read a skein.

pages.t: Omens are rare changes of the world: once every few days something happens and lasts from a minute to a day. Each comes where its current is — to murky water, to a living workshop, to Gauge Stones, in a storm or at sunset — and each has an answer in your hands and a reward right at the danger. Witness an omen and it is written here on its own page: what it is, how to answer it, what it rewards.
World events are switched off by the world rule "World events", cult raids by their own rule "Cult raids"; on a server it is decided for everyone, in single player by you.

The Procession of the Sunken comes to murky water by your workshop at night after rain: the Mirebearer carries a living mire tussock on its back and plants it in the water, where a new knot of mire will rise. Cleanse the water before they arrive and the procession turns back; break all of it while the tussock is still on its back and it dries into silt, and the Keener sometimes drops a Sunken Lament. Every three to six days, to whoever has studied "Mire"; a clean neighborhood does not call the raid.

The Toll Collection comes by day to a Gauge Stone you attuned: the Bailiff drives a Toll Tap into it, and three chunks around dry to the bottom of the bed. Strike the Bailiff down while he kneels at the stone and the Collection fails, leaving you a Toll Reliquary of drunk flux; too late, and you break the tap, and the flux returns in a splash. Every three to six days.

The Rounds of the Still are a threat to your workshop with a reward: at sunset the Order comes to a living workshop — where flux is drawn and still runs full — to stop it, and leaves still grains to whoever meets it. A Still Pane rises by the workshop: for twenty seconds it sets, and the Stillness shows through it. Thaw it with a Thaw Lantern within eight blocks or with quickwater, or break it with three blows, and there will be no raid, and grains are left by the pane. Too late, and the squad comes out: the Bellringer walks to the middle of the workshop to read the stone rite, while the Vowkeeper and the Clockbound guard him. A full-strength blow breaks the rite and it starts over; a squad broken before the stone leaves more grains, sometimes a Rule as well. Finish the rite, and a Halt Stone rises: in 3 × 3 chunks no device can draw flux until the stone is broken or a day has passed. Every four to seven days, until the Restart.

The Hour's Hitch is a gift and an alarm at once: at sunset the world falls into the Stillness's beat for three minutes, and Stilled people appear near you — their still memories and grains otherwise come only from the Stillness and from Snarls. The sun stands at the horizon, stars show by day, the light holds at sunset, and the flux in the world neither flows nor refills — use what you have. A Thaw Lantern within eight blocks or quickwater lets a person finish their step: they speak a line and leave a Still Memory, and every third one rises as a Laggard; a pickaxe breaks one into still grains. The untouched crumble once the sun moves on. Every seven to twelve days, for everyone in the world, if someone has seen the Stillness.

The Murk Storm strikes where the flux has stagnated: in a thunderstorm near a murky workshop, every twenty to forty seconds a murk discharge hits a murky chunk nearby — with no fire, so buildings do not burn. Two or three seconds before the strike a ring of runes cracks and hisses on the ground: step away. A lightning rod within thirty-two blocks catches the discharge and grounds it — six tenths of the chunk's murk turns into flux, so the storm cleans your workshop for free; on open ground the discharge burns murk away, but where murk is above half the bed and flux is being drawn, a Snarl is born; a Snarl nearby twists tighter unless it has a Weir. Whoever is caught takes three damage and Silting. A clean neighborhood does not call the Murk Storm. Every three to five days, for whoever has studied "Snarl".

The Upwelling is a night threat with a find: the Lees lie right under the water, and sometimes the bottom breathes out — a Lees Boil wells up on the bed of water near you. For ten minutes it raises murk in the chunk (up to three quarters of the bed: above a third, mire grows, and the Procession of the Sunken finds murky water), and Murk Fry rise from the bottom. Cap the boil: a Lumenash Grate in the stack above it (on the bottom and up to two blocks higher) clogs with silt in half a minute and dampens it by a third; a working Purifier in the chunk counts as a grate once a minute. Three thirds and the boil is capped, and finds float up from the bottom: Lees Shells, Bedsilt, sometimes Niello and a Murky Geode; rinse the clogged grates in running water as usual. A Sounding Lead thrown into the surface over a live boil raises a Whirlpool at once — a short way down to the Lees. An uncapped boil dies down on its own and leaves the murk behind. Every four to seven days, at night, for whoever has been to the Lees.

The Murkflow is a Lees threat with loot in its crest: murk flows in the Lees, and sometimes a surge drives it along the bottom. A wall of haze rises on one side and moves past you as a straight front, a block a second — a mod line tells you where it comes from. Whoever it engulfs gets Silting while inside (about ten seconds), and the fog closes in to twenty blocks; every chunk on its way gets three murk (the bed murk pulls it back by itself), and mire grows thicker there. The Murkflow passes the Bright Shallows and a chunk with a working Purifier by: one murk and no Silting — the lesson of a Clean Camp. Things of the bottom tumble in its crest — Lees Shells, Niello, Silt, Murky Geodes, rarely a still grain: strike one with a Pike Pole, as you would a Snarl's kink, and it flies to you; whatever is not snatched leaves with the front. Every twenty-five to forty minutes in the Lees, outside the Bright Shallows.

The Skeining gives you a new skein — born before your eyes, once every five to eight days, and you decide how it winds. By living water (a river, a swamp, a jungle), where the flux runs full and the murk stays below a third of the bed, the streams of the eight nearby chunks reach for a point above the water and twist like yarn on fingers: for the first minute they gather, for three minutes the bud grows, in the last one the threads draw tight, and a skein hangs above the water. A full vial of distillate poured on the bud makes its current a native thread — up to three, in place of the place's weakest threads; opposite Springs without Lattice wind a turbulent skein, Murk from a vial a murky one. Keep the water clean: murk at a third of the bed by the bud for twenty seconds winds a murky skein; draw no flux in the 3 × 3 chunks — ten seconds of work nearby make it greedy. A Lumenash nearby sometimes gives a lucent skein. Its size follows how full the chunks stayed: full gives a medium one, sometimes large; drunk dry, a small one. Go farther than sixty-four blocks and the bud unravels without a trace.

The Roll Call fills your workshop with flux and gives Channel Records — at a clear midnight the Gauge Stones check each other, as in the Reckoners' days. It needs your attuned stone and at least one more within a hundred and twenty-eight blocks. Yours answers first, then the others in turn: on each, the Marked Tiles light up from the bottom, and a thread of light runs to the nearest stone that has answered — the network of beds becomes visible. For two minutes the seams of these stones carry flux three times faster, and while you stay by your stone (within thirty-two blocks), the flux around each answering stone gathers to your workshop — their chunks never drop below six tenths of the bed. Read an answering stone with a Loupe — three times in ten it gives a Channel Record, no more than two per Roll Call. There is no danger. Every four to six days, for whoever has studied "Gauge Stones".

The Living Minute is a minute of flux in a world without flux, and still grains from the sky. The hand of the motionless hour sometimes slips by one mark: for whoever has spent half an hour to three quarters of an hour in the Stillness, outside a lantern's circle and the Thawed, the Stillness moves for a minute. Within forty-eight blocks of you the bed is sixteen: the Conduit, the Flux Workbench and devices work without their own store, and still skeins give up their threads — hurry to cast, craft and fill. Six to nine still grains fall from the sky within twenty-four blocks — frost flashes on the ground for a moment where a grain will land; gather them. Sentinels within forty-eight blocks wake and come for you, and if there are none, one steps out of its half-step: leave or meet it. The water stays glass, no block thaws. A click — and everything stands: the minute's flux is gone, the hand goes back.

The Spillover gives eight minutes of a rare current of place and full chunks: a Quickstream race spills over the brim of its bed and flows across the sky above the surroundings of someone who has been to the Quickstream. Under it — within sixteen blocks of its trace on the ground — the bed is 1.4 times as deep, and the current of place is the race's current: the Flux Workbench pays with it, Current Seeds grow by it, skeins wind their threads twice as fast, murk is carried away; fill a Flux Reservoir and a Belt Reliquary. A race can carry any current; the "guest" ones — Soul, Tempo, Echo, Halo — come more often. Climb up to it — with a Grapnel up a hill or a tree beneath it, with a Vane or Freshet Mantle, on a pillar of blocks — and it carries you like the races of the Quickstream: crouch to ride slowly, step out sideways with the movement keys. Schools of racefish stand in the race against its run — read them with a Loupe up close: that is how its current is discovered. In the last ten seconds the race lowers whoever it carries gently, and the flux above the bed flows off to the neighbors. There is no danger: it is a gift, but a short one. Every seven to twelve days.

The Racefish Run gives readings and rare currents: at dawn, for whoever has read a race, schools of light-fish swim up a clean river nearby — the bed of every chunk is a branch of the Quickstream, and its fish go up the branches. Each school carries its own current — the current of the place, and sometimes a guest one that never occurs here; some also carry one of the currents it is made of. Come within five blocks of a school and read it with a Loupe — that is how rare currents are discovered. Where a school has passed, the river freshens: flux rises by a twentieth of the bed, murk falls by a third. A murky river — murk from a sixth of the bed — turns the schools back: keep the river clean. A racefish cannot be caught: a blow, a hook and a bucket do not take it, it fades into light. Two to four schools over four minutes, every three to five days.

The Turn of the Wheel grants a day of unusual currents of place — and takes the usual ones away: the Tollkeepers in the Quickstream spin the Toll Wheel with the flux they have drunk, and from dawn to dawn the Springs of every place stand one step further along the Wheel — Tide reads as Strata, Strata as Ember, Ember as Gale, Gale as Tide. By a river the current of place is Strata, in a desert it is Gale; the Poles and the combined currents, items and creatures stay the same. Use it: a Flux Workbench recipe or Current Seeds that lacked a Spring of the place will come together today; or wait it out — a Brimming Jug by a river is silent for the day. A Loupe on the place says the Wheel is turned. At the start of the day a wheel shows in the sky and turns a quarter, at the end it turns back. Defeat a Tollfarmer at his Toll Barrage and the Wheel is never turned again. Every eight to twelve days, for everyone in the world, if someone has met the Tollkeepers.

The Peddler's Visit brings what is far to fetch: every three to five days by day, a Snagling Peddler with a laden Driftback comes to whoever has started the Codex — saplings and herbs of distant places, a rare find such as a Current Hank, and a map to a ruin. He trades with anyone, without gifts, for things carrying his craved Spring; with a Kin Knot, at half price. He stays a day where he came out and leaves; strike him and he takes offense and leaves at once. There is no danger.

nodes.hint: The world sometimes changes for a while. Witness one of the omens — a Procession, a Toll Collection, an Hour's Hitch.

pages.t: Hour Marks go into the Dawn and Dusk Pillars, the Winding Key and the Dead Dial of the Great Pendulum, and the Full Moon Mark into the Full-Moon Apple; two different marks at the Desk play the Hour Check technique: the next lock and aqueduct on the board cost no notes. Once you study this entry, the Loupe learns to catch the hour: raise it to the open sky at its hour and hold it as when reading — with a sheet of paper in your inventory, it writes a mark. You need not wait for the hour every time: a mark you already have is copied at the Flux Workbench.

The hours of the day: dawn while the sun rises, noon when it stands highest, dusk while it sets, midnight in the dead of night; each hour's window lasts under two minutes. All night the Loupe also writes the Moon — full, waning, new or waxing, whichever is in the sky; at midnight two marks come out at once. Each mark is written once a day: the same sky will not give it twice. The line under the Loupe's sight says which hour is open, how long until the next one and whether it is written today.

An hour exists only under a sky where days pass: under a roof or underground the Loupe reads the place, not the hour; in the Nether and the End no mark comes out, and the Stillness stands in the still hour — marks for its Pendulum are brought from the ordinary world. The Reckoners measured Tempo by the sky: their Gauge Stones struck the hours by these same marks, and village gaugers still buy Noon Marks.

Copying a mark: at the Flux Workbench, lay a mark over a sheet of paper — the same mark comes out, and the original stays in the grid; it spends the sheet and 6 flux, the sun's hours ask for Ember in the place, midnight and the Moon for Tide. With Shift you get one copy per sheet. A copy is as good as a caught mark: recipes, the Dead Dial and the Hour Check take it. The first mark of each kind still has to be caught in the sky.

kp: Отметка полудня Noon Mark Отметка полудня Noon Mark
nodes.hint: Reveal Tempo and Gleam with the Loupe and solve the puzzle at the Desk — the Loupe will learn to catch the hour in the sky.

pages.t: Both trees work for a fluxionist. A living weeping willow by water raises the flux of its chunk 1.35 times — by a workshop, where the Workbench and devices draw flux from the land, there is more of it. A lumenash with living leaves turns the murk of its chunk into flux — 0.02 a second per trunk, up to three trunks a chunk: plant lumenash where murk settles. Both woods make planks, stairs and slabs, and the herbs of the currents grow under the trees and by water — read each one with the Loupe and its page opens here.

The weeping willow grows in swamps and along rivers, lakes and brooks — no farther than ten blocks from water. Its trunk leans, its branches arch, strands hang from its clouds of leaves down to the ground: shears take them whole. One willow in eight is old and hollow: its foot is swollen, with a slit in it, and inside lie a Reckoner coffer that a gauger hid by the water and a Glint Nest where curls of glint flame still glow in the strands. At night the hollow glows through the slit. A willow grown from a sapling never gets a hollow: only old ones have it.

The lumenash grows rarely and alone — in woods, plains and meadows, more often in the Weeping Floodplain. Its leaves glow and flicker with Gleam, samaras fall from its twigs. A trunk clears murk only while living leaves stand over it: a felled lumenash clears nothing. The oldest of them — the Elder Lumenash with a skein in its hollow — is told of in the entry "Skeins".

The planks of any tree of the currents — willow, lumenash, mirebound planks and the trees of the places — make a boat: it goes on water like a boat of the game and carries two. Five planks in a trough at a crafting table; a boat and a chest make a boat with chest of twenty-seven slots. Each has the Drift sign carved on its bow, filled with resin the color of its wood.

Rippleleaf is Tide in a body of grass (Tide 3, Root 1): on the Crucible's quiet heat it dissolves into Tide with no stone and no water. The herbalist's Herb Mortar grinds it into two cyan dyes, it goes into the Fish Trap, and a herbalist buys ten for an emerald. It grows at the very edge of water — swamps, rivers, beaches, woods and plains; rings of ripples run over its leaves.

Emberbell is Ember that does not burn your hands (Ember 3, Gleam 1, Root 1): on the Crucible's quiet heat it dissolves into Ember. The mortar grinds it into two orange dyes, a herbalist buys six for an emerald. It grows by lava in caves, on deepslate and basalt, and smolders dimly in the dark — by it you know there is lava round the bend.

Murkcap is a sign of murk you can see without the Loupe: flakes of it rise over the cap (Murk 2, Gloom 1, Root 1). Where it grows, the flux has stood still: plant lumenash there, not a workshop. The mortar grinds it into a purple dye, a herbalist buys four for an emerald, and in the smoke of a Murk Fumer the game's mushrooms turn into murkcaps. It grows in dark damp caves — by water, on silt, clay and moss.

kp: Willow, Ash and Herbs Ива, ясень и травы

nodes.hint: Two trees of the currents grow in the world: the weeping willow by water and the lumenash in woods. Read one.

pages.t: The three crafts of the river villages trade in what a fluxionist needs early: the gauger sells opaline, Knotted Cords and Reckoner Records, the herbalist a shard of their region's current, saplings and Bloom Tonic, the lamplighter float lanterns and Fisher's Chowder, and buys glint wisps. Their houses stand in the game's ordinary villages; an unemployed villager takes a Wax Kettle, Clepsydra or Herb Mortar you set down and learns the craft. The workplaces are useful without a villager too.

The lamplighter sets float lanterns on the river at sunset and spears fish by their light. Buys honeycomb, salmon and glint wisps; sells candles, lanterns, cooked salmon, a float lantern in the color of their region, Fisher's Chowder, spectral arrows, a Pike Pole and a Ford Wolf Tuft, and a master sells a firefly lantern and a Flux Pebble. The Wax Kettle melts honeycomb into wax and dips string into a candle: two candles from one comb, and the little fire under it never goes out.

The gauger measures the river's rise and the hours with knots on a cord — the Reckoners' knot writing. Buys paper, string, copper, raw antimony, amethyst shards and Noon Marks; sells a book and quill, a compass, a clock, opaline, a Knotted Cord, concentrates from the gauge rod, a spyglass, and a master sells a bell and Reckoner Records from the village chronicle: a Record you read goes into the Codex as notes. The Clepsydra is a clock for a comparator: sixteen marks of the day from sunrise, a chime at sunrise, noon, sunset and midnight.

The herbalist gathers the herbs that grow along the flux and plants lumenash by the village so that murk does not settle by the houses. Buys Rippleleaf, Emberbell, Murkcap and glass bottles; sells glow berries, a weeping willow sapling, Bloom Tonic, Silt, a shard of their region's current, a glistering melon slice, and a master sells a lumenash sapling and a distillate vial. The Herb Mortar grinds a bone into four bone meal and a flower or herb of the currents into twice the dye.

kp: Восковой котелок Wax Kettle Клепсидра Clepsydra Травяная ступка Herb Mortar Клепсидра Clepsydra
nodes.hint: Lamplighters, gaugers and herbalists live in villages by rivers. Read their workplace with the Loupe — a kettle, a clepsydra or a mortar.

pages.t: A Fair Copy gives a friend everything your Codex knows, at once: a friend joins when you are already at the Stillness — and need not start from Quickdust. Take a clean copy in hand and press it on a Reckoning Desk with your Codex on it: your studied entries (boards as solved), revealed currents and Loupe readings are copied in. Give the copy to your friend: they take it in hand and right-click — the knowledge becomes theirs, and the copy turns clean again.

Notes are not copied: your friend keeps their own, and things you have already read with the Loupe will give them no notes. Filling a copy takes half a pen of Ruling Pen ink (48 divisions); your own filled copy can be filled again with fresh knowledge. Entries you took in from someone else's copy are not copied on: only what you studied yourself is passed. Entries with Dissonance give the reader half their Dissonance, 10 at most. Your deeds — the first step into the Stillness, victories, Dissonance thresholds — are each one's own.

The Reckoners copied their records fair and handed them to apprentices: an apprentice who read the master's fair copy knew all the master knew, and the book came back clean — for the next one. The ink of a fair copy flows like the Codex's — that is why the knowledge leaves the page for whoever reads it.

kp: Беловик Fair Copy Беловик Fair Copy
nodes.hint: Your whole Codex can be copied fair and handed to a friend. The task waits at the Reckoning Desk.

pages.t: The Snaglings trade with those they take in as kin — Bolas, Catch Bundles, ore concentrate and opaline, Reckoner Records and Flux Pebbles — and let their kin into the Catch Heap in the middle of the camp. They pay and take not in emeralds but in craving: each band craves one Spring, and only things carrying that Spring are worth anything to it. The Loupe over a Snagling names its band's craving, and the beads on its ears glow its color.

How to become kin: bring the band gifts to its craving — drop a thing nearby (they will pick it up) or hand it over. A gift is worth the number of the craved Spring in the thing's currents, for the whole stack: Tide 2 for a cod, Ember 3 for coal, Strata 2 for cobblestone, Gale 1 for bamboo. The band takes you in for 32 of its craving; twice that while it holds a grudge, half with a Kin Knot in your inventory — the first band to take you in gives you one. From your hand a Snagling takes only what carries the craving, but from the ground it picks up anything, so mind what you drop. The band pours back at your feet whatever it took from you that was not a gift, and never touches your things again.

Grudges: strike a Snagling, kill one, or open or break the Catch Heap as a stranger, and the whole band around holds a grudge for 10 minutes, 20 for a killing. A band with a grudge fights. A Gleaner's hook snatches one thing from the stack in your hand and it runs — catch it and strike it, and it drops it. A Charmer ties a knot over your hand: switch the slot and the knot has nothing to hold, or the thing slips out toward it. A Snarer whirls Bolas over its head — step aside or into cover: Bolas slow you for 2.5 seconds and stop you jumping. The band never touches its kin.

Trade: for kin, a right click opens trade, and each kind has its own goods. The Gleaner — with a huge creel and a hook pole — sells what the river brings: Silt, ore concentrate, opaline, glint wisps, Catch Bundles, Records and a Flux Pebble. The Charmer — in a tall twisted cap, with a rattle — sells the Knotted Cord (the Reckoners' knot-script came from the Snaglings), Current Seeds, Bloom Tonic and glow ink. The Snarer — in a bark mask — sells Bolas, a Ford Wolf Tuft, a rabbit's foot, spectral arrows and a Pike Pole. The stock comes back by dawn. They take payment in things carrying the craved Spring: the costly goods in shards of that Spring.

The peddler: every three to five days by day a Snagling Peddler comes out to you on his own — under a creel taller than his head, in a wide straw hat, with a staff, and a laden Driftback on a lead behind him. He is the only one of his folk who trades with strangers, without gifts: saplings and herbs of distant places, one rare find (a Current Hank, Glowsilk, Catch Bundles) and one map to a ruin — a Snagling camp, a Reckoner Lock or a Fallen Gauge Stone, marked with a red cross as a cartographer's map is. He takes things carrying his craved Spring (the Loupe names it under his name), the costly goods in shards; with a Kin Knot in your inventory, at half price. His stock does not come back. He stays a day where he came out and slips away into the reeds; strike him and he takes offense and leaves at once.

Where to look: the Snaglings' home is the Rustling Fens, where most of them live; wandering bands of two to four also walk the Weeping Floodplain, jungles, swamps and mushroom fields by day, but never a murky chunk — murk is a catch gone bad to them. Snagling camps stand in clearings: three shelters, a catch pole with lanterns, a fire, and in the middle the Catch Heap, the band's hoard, which opens like a chest for kin. Camp dwellers do not stray far from it.

In the Rustling Fens stand the Snaglings' stiltholds, and there is all you need for a hut of your own: Osier Rods cut with shears from the heads of pollard osiers (they grow back in the light) for the Wicker Block, Wicker Mat, Wattle Fence and Wicker Lantern; Tall Sedge for Reed Thatch; lightrush, whose fluff smolders with light; peat for fuel; bog oak, a black wood found only in the world; pebblework from the shoals. The fens are a delta where the mangrove swamps were, where flux runs thick and wild; whatever broke off upstream settles here in the reeds. The stiltholds stand over the channels on bog-oak stilts, the Catch Heap on a deck. The Reckoners measured the fens with weirs, and the Snaglings took them apart for stone — by a dismantled weir a coffer still lies under the water.

"What flows is no one's," the Snaglings say. Everything in the world is a current gone still, and everything chips off: a splinter, a feather, a fish, a dropped thing — a current drifting to whoever catches it. The Snaglings took against the Reckoners, who came to measure the currents: what is measured is no longer a catch, it has an owner. Thieves they call only the Tollkeepers, who take a share of every current. And the Snaglings' fearful tale is the Stillness, where nothing drifts and there is nothing to catch.

nodes.hint: A small folk that picks up whatever lies about lives in the Rustling Fens, weeping floodplains, jungles and swamps. Read a Snagling or the fens with the Loupe.

pages.t: The Inkpine Forest gives a fluxionist three things. Ink Resin refills a Ruling Pen fully on a crafting table — no current shard needed, and in the Crucible it is the richest living source of Gloom. Scrollbark goes into paper and into Scroll Shelves, which power an enchanting table like bookshelves. And deep in the forest stands the Reckoner Scriptorium, where their Records lie.

Resin is taken by hand: an inkpine's bark sometimes bears a wound with a bead of ink — use it and the resin is yours; in time the wound seeps again. Scrollbark lifts in sheets: cut a loose sheet with shears, and the next one peels by itself. The forest grows where old-growth taiga would: look for black spires hung with silver lichen and water nearly black.

The Scriptorium is a library of two floors: bays of scroll shelves, a gallery, a bell tower with an inkwell lamp, a fallen wing with ink vats. The scribes sealed the reading room and left the order in the bays themselves: the rule by the door says how to read it. At night Inkblots rise in the forest — ink that was never let to settle — and Hush Owls fly without a sound. A Copyist's Lodge by the path keeps a store of resin and bark.

kp: Свитковая полка Scroll Shelf Лампа-чернильница Inkwell Lamp Чернильная смола Ink Resin
nodes.hint: The Reckoners' library forest: resin, bark and Records. Read an inkpine, its resin or the place itself with the Loupe.

pages.t: The Smolderwood gives Ember without going down to the lava: in its Ember Seams, ember crystals grow right at the surface, and in the caves below every second crystal nest is Ember. Here too are wood that does not burn (smolder pine planks), dark Kilnstone for a house, Smolder Coal that burns twice as long as coal, and the Tollkeepers' kiln camps.

At night an Ember Seam shows from afar: a crack in the ground glowing orange. Hot ash lies along its rim: it burns like magma — walk around it or sneak across. Inside are Emberstone and ember crystals: a pickaxe takes shards from a crystal, Kilnstone and now and then a shard from Emberstone. Walk out of the crack toward its ends, where it is shallow.

Fallen brands give light (6) and set nothing alight; an axe splits a brand into one or two Smolder Coal, Silk Touch takes it whole. Smolder Coal burns in a furnace for 3200 ticks. A Kiln Brazier gives light 15. Fire does not spread in the Smolderwood: nothing that grows here burns, and fire brought in dies down sooner. Brandlings lie among the brands — smaller living brands with dim eyes: they rise against whoever comes close or chops a brand nearby, bite with fire, and when slain lie down as brands again. Water puts them out.

Centuries ago the Ember vein set this forest alight from below, and fire here flows slowly, like resin: embers smolder in the cracks of the black pines, coals rise from the ground, and at night ember moths gather to the smoldering trunks. The Tollkeepers came to take a toll from the fire too: their kiln camps — domed kilns of fired brick with reliquaries of Ember — are guarded by Toll Collectors and a Bailiff.

nodes.hint: A forest that has smoldered for centuries. Read the empty air of the Smolderwood, a brand or an Emberstone with the Loupe.

pages.t: The Honeyfall Grove gives Tempo — a rare current — straight off the trees. An amber bead swells on the ripe bark of a honey maple: take it with an empty hand — that is honey resin (Tempo 2, Craft 1). The scar beads again in about half an hour to an hour. Only grown maples give resin: a log placed by hand does not. At dusk the beads glow, so ripe maples show from afar. Tempo goes into freshet steel in the Crucible, the Quickened Thought of automata, the Tempo glyph and the gear of the hour.

Where to look: in place of a birch forest — dark maples with tiers of amber leaves, a golden haze, dry gold grass. Umberstone lies in boulders and shows on slopes: it gives bricks, sundial tiles and the chiseled dial. Foxfire glows in fallen maples (light 6), honey mushrooms at the roots (light 3). The hourbloom is open by day and folded at night; bees love it. The Honey Lantern (light 14) is made of maple planks, resin and a honey mushroom.

Beware at night: heaps of leaves lie in the litter, and in some a cream vein smolders — that is a Leafwight. Come within four blocks and it rises, and its touch steals Tempo: for three seconds you are slow. Wounded, it loses leaves that hang in the air for a breath. Killed, it drops a Lingering Leaf — Tempo for the Crucible as well.

The Reckoners' clockmakers slowed Tempo here by a hair to count it, and it never sped up again: in the grove it is forever the last hour of autumn, leaves fall slowly, and some hang for a breath. The clockmakers left observatories; later fluxionists came to the warm quiet groves and built homesteads — and left in turn.

kp: Медвяный фонарь Honey Lantern Медвяная смола Honey Resin
nodes.hint: A grove where you pick Tempo off the bark by hand. Read the Honeyfall Grove, a honey maple or honey resin with the Loupe.

pages.t: The clockmakers' sphere is their way of measuring Tempo and a centrepiece for your study: brass rings of the equator, the meridian and the ecliptic around a cream heart of Tempo (light 5), with sparks running along the rings. You know an observatory by its round tower of umber bricks under a green copper dome and the sundial in its yard; on the gallery stand a Reckoner coffer and the clockmaker's journal.

The clockmakers were the branch of the Reckoners that measured Tempo. To count it they slowed it — and decided that a slowed current is better than a living one: what is stopped does not spoil. The Order of the Still Hour grew out of the clockmakers. The grove where they learned still lives in their last hour.

kp: Армиллярная сфера Armillary Sphere Армиллярная сфера Armillary Sphere
nodes.hint: Read the Armillary Sphere in a Clockmakers' Observatory within the Honeyfall Grove with the Loupe.

pages.t: The Sanguine Weald gives Bloom without brewing. Sap veins glow on the bark of old sanguine aspens: a bottle at such a vein fills with heartsap (Bloom 3, Soul 1), and the vein heals and fills again in a few days. Heartsap goes into the Crucible and tonics; drunk like honey, it heals for a couple of heartbeats.

Where to look: in place of a dark forest — a crimson canopy over pale trunks, dusk beneath it and almost black leafmold. Every eight seconds all the veins of the weald flash at once — that beat gives it away. Candlecaps on the trunks are light without torches: plant them on any log. Sanguine slate and the dark wine aspen planks make a dark warm house. Heartsap and planks make the Heartsap Lamp.

The weald soaked up a beat that was never allowed to happen. When the founder of the Order gave his Tempo to the Great Stilling, his heart stopped first, and the beat went out as a wave of Bloom through the ground. The old forest drank it: life rushed into the crowns and could flow no further. They say the Order set a ring somewhere in the weald to stop the beat.

kp: Лампада рдяного сока Heartsap Lamp Рдяный сок Heartsap
nodes.hint: A forest where you fill a bottle with Bloom. Read the Sanguine Weald, its aspen or heartsap with the Loupe.

pages.t: The Grottoes are a mine of currents. Crystal nests are three times as many here, and each of the six bases is equally likely: all four Sources for the first Quickdust in one cave. Flowstone lies here by itself, without a shard — take the floor with a pickaxe. Cave pearls glow on the bottom of the rimstone pools (Prism 2, Tide, Halo) — for the Crucible and for the light of the Pearl Lamp; the caddis of the pools shed them now and then, and a water bucket carries a caddis home to your own pool. The onyx in the bands of the walls is a dark stone for a house.

Where to look: deep under gentle lands far inland, where dripstone caves would otherwise be. The floor is Flowstone in steps of rimstone pools, the walls have bands of dark onyx, cream drips grow from the ceiling and the floor, glowing flux veins run over the stone. The light is small: drip tips, veins, moss, pearls — bring your own. A drip hurts whoever falls on it, and one cut from above falls. Deeper in the Grottoes stand the Reckoners' Wells.

Under the uplands an underground vein of flux runs through the rock, and where it comes up to a cave the stone itself begins to flow: everything in the world is a frozen current, and here it thaws. The Reckoners found these places first and sank their Wells into them, to gauge the world's flux right at the stone. Their marks on the shaft walls can still be read.

kp: Жемчужная лампада Pearl Lamp Пещерная жемчужина Cave Pearl
nodes.hint: Caves where the stone flows. Read the empty air of the Grottoes, a drip, a flux vein or a pearl with the Loupe.

pages.t: Silt Herons keep the mire of the Stagnant Backwater in check: they spear Mire Leeches and Murk Gnats and cough up a lump of Silt after every three meals. Where they wade, there are fewer mire creatures. A running step makes a heron take off and glide away; creep up crouching, and it stays. It stands on one leg for a long time and is easy to take for a gray snag.

At night a light glows over the still water — do not trust it. Glints are never born of a swamp, only of a Crucible; this light has a murky heart and hangs on a stalk. It is the lure of a Mire Angler: whoever comes within six steps it grabs with a lunge from the water, and the bite silts. A crouching player it notices only three steps away. On land the angler is clumsy and easy to hurt — lure it ashore. It drops Silt, and sometimes a glow ink sac.

kp: Life of the Backwater Жители заводи
Яйцо призыва: илистая цапля Silt Heron Spawn Egg
nodes.hint: Something lives in the still water. Read a Silt Heron or a Mire Angler with the Loupe.

pages.t: The Lumenhart gives Lumenash Charcoal without a single lumenash felled: every five to ten minutes an adult sheds a Lumenhart Antler, and a Flux Forge burns the antler into charcoal for brightsteel. Lumenash trees clean the murk — better leave them growing. The deer walk in herds and follow Rippleleaf held in hand; startle one, and you startle them all. At night the buds on their antlers glow.

At night Willowkin step out of the strands of the weeping willows and walk the grove. They leave you be while you leave the grove be: fell a willow or a lumenash at night, and every Willowkin within twenty-four steps comes for you; their blow lashes with strands and binds the legs. At dawn a Willowkin takes root and grows into a willow sapling — that is how the floodplain regrows by itself.

kp: Life of the Floodplain Жители поймы
nodes.hint: Deer with branching antlers graze the Weeping Floodplain, and at night something walks among the willows. Read a Lumenhart, a Willowkin or a Lumenhart Antler with the Loupe.

pages.t: For a hall, a garden or a square: eight statues from the lore of the flux and its cults, six stained glasses of the six primal currents, 3 × 3 windows with one picture — the Wheel rose and two pictures — and four planters that take any flowers, saplings and mushrooms. All of it is made on an ordinary crafting table and lies in the Decor tab. Each statue keeps one feature glowing at night; stained glass joins into one window without seams.

A statue is two blocks tall and faces you when placed. The Fluxionist holds a Loupe to the eye — its lens glows; the notches of the Reckoner's gauge rod smolder; the stones of the four Springs glow on the Wheel — Gale above, Tide to the right, Strata below, Ember to the left; bronze palms raise a glint.
A statue is a trophy: the stone of the figure, its token and a pedestal of flowstone bricks. The Wheel needs shards of the four Springs, the glint statue a bottled glint.

Stained glass is eight glass and a shard of its current: the waves of Tide, the layers of malachite, the tongues of Ember, the streams of Gale, the diamonds of Lattice, the shattered glass of Fray. The pattern runs on into the next block, and now and then a roundel with the rune of the current appears in the window. Six stained glass make sixteen panes.
A planter is like a flower pot, but for any plant: click with a plant to plant it, with an empty hand to take it back. A glowing plant glows in the planter too, and a broken planter drops it.

The Wheel Rose Window is a 3 × 3 window with one picture: place nine blocks in a square in a wall and the Wheel appears across the whole window — the four Springs, the hoop of the other currents and the Poles at the hub. A block on its own is plain amber glass; break one and the picture falls apart, put it back and it appears again. At night the rose glows softly from within.

The pictures go up like the rose: nine blocks in a square in a wall. The Stillness Clock has its hands stopped at five to six over frozen water; in the Snagling Catch a fish, a feather and opaline drift to whoever snags them. Windows of different pictures never merge. At night the pictures glow faintly.

Statues of the three cults and of a Snagling elder are trophies of their places: the Still with a bell and a wound mechanism in its chest, the Tollkeeper with a reliquary of drunk currents, the Sunken with a boathook and murky eyes, the elder with a staff where a Tide pod glows.
The Sunken needs a Murk Flask and Silt; the elder a Knotted Cord, bog oak and a Tide shard.
The speculum planter is made of speculum sheets, the opaline one of opaline on a bronze stem.

kp: Statues, Stained Glass and Planters Статуи, витражи и кашпо

Статуя флюксиониста Fluxionist Statue Статуя Исчислителя Reckoner Statue Статуя Колеса Wheel Statue Статуя огонька Glint Statue Витраж Прилива Tide Stained Glass Витражная панель Прилива Tide Stained Glass Pane Кашпо из Струйчатого камня Flowstone Planter Ивовое кашпо Willow Planter Розетка Колеса Wheel Rose Window Окно «Часы Застылья» Stillness Clock Window Окно «Улов коряжников» Snagling Catch Window Статуя Недвижного Statue of the Still Статуя Мытаря Tollkeeper Statue Статуя Донного Statue of the Sunken Статуя старейшины коряжников Snagling Elder Statue Бронзовое кашпо Speculum Planter Опаловое кашпо Opaline Planter Статуя Колеса Wheel Statue
nodes.hint: A fluxionist's house wants beauty. Read glass or a flower pot.

pages.t: The Marking Watch takes you back a minute: click it, and a mark is set where you stand; click again or wait a minute — and you are there again, with the health and hunger you had at the mark. Before a risky jump, a descent into a lair or a sortie over the edge, it is your way back. Things and the world do not go back: what you took stays with you, what you broke stays broken.

Only you can see the mark: a pale rune of Tempo on the ground, and an arc runs down its ring — the time left until the return; the bar under the watch shows the same. After a return the watch rests five minutes; a return leaves a Ripple unless you are under the Hush. The mark breaks without a return if you leave its world, die, there is no room to stand at it, or in the Stillness — if it or you are off thawed ground.

kp: Засечка Marking Watch Засечка Marking Watch
nodes.hint: A Clockmakers' watch that takes you back a minute.

pages.t: The Toll Cleaver strikes harder than a netherite sword and speeds your step in hand — but every blow takes a toll. Where the land is alive, the toll is hardly felt: half a unit of the flux of the chunk you stand in. Where the land is dry — on banks drunk by the Tollkeepers, in murky places — the cleaver takes blood: a heart a blow, but never below one heart. It is found in the barrels of Toll Posts.

The cleaver takes blood past your armor: it is a payment, not a blow, and neither the Rewind Weight nor the Last-Minute Watch notices it. With mastery the flux toll grows lighter, the blood toll becomes half a heart, and at last a killing blow gives change: it gives a heart back. The Tollkeepers forged such blades to take a share of every current they cut.

nodes.hint: The Tollkeepers' blade takes a toll from every blow. Read it with the Loupe.

pages.t: The Crucible is the heart of alchemy: things dissolve in it into currents, and from currents new things are brewed — fluxsteel, wax, opaline, quickdust, tonics and glints. It is neither forged nor put together on a workbench — it is woken. A pinch of quickdust on a plain cauldron, and the iron remembers that it once flowed: the cauldron grows heavy with old bronze, its feet turn into beast's paws, and opaline surfaces along the rim.

Pour a bucket of water into the Crucible — that is its full measure. A full bucket can be scooped back out, but whatever has dissolved splashes out as murk; a broken Crucible spills it the same way. To clear the Crucible without losing the water, use it with an empty hand while sneaking: the distillate sloshes over the rim, its currents sink into the land around as murk, and the water stays clean.

Without heat the Crucible is just a bowl: whatever you throw in lies on the bottom. The fire beneath decides what dissolves. Gentle heat — a campfire, fire, magma, a lit furnace — takes soft things: herbs, flesh, coal, dust, wax. Strong heat — lava — takes everything that has currents in it.

Hard things are those where Strata, Alloy and Prism make up half the currents or more: metal, stone, glass, gems. In gentle heat they do not sink — they bob up and leap over the rim. That way iron is never lost in a Crucible over a campfire.

Water boils away: a bucket lasts sixteen minutes over gentle heat and eight over strong, and every thing that dissolves drinks a little more. Let it boil dry, and the distillate scorches and goes to murk entirely. A thing with no currents never sinks at all.

Crucible recipes call for a catalyst — the thing thrown in last, once the distillate holds what is needed. If it matches, the recipe's currents are spent, and the result bobs up and leaps over the rim. If not, the catalyst dissolves like any other thing.

nodes.hint: A pot in which things dissolve into currents. Read a cauldron and water with the Loupe; water, herbs and flowers bring notes of Alchemy.

pages.t: This entry keeps your Crucible free of murk: whoever knows which currents get along brews without loss. A dissolved thing does not vanish: its currents pass into the water and become distillate — current in liquid form. Distillate takes the color of its blend, and strands of the strongest currents wind through it. Aim the Loupe at the Crucible, and its Distillate line shows the runes and how much of each.
Neighbors on the Wheel get along: Tide with Strata, Strata with Ember, Ember with Gale, Gale with Tide all enter the distillate whole. Compound currents blend with anything without loss.

Opposite Springs — Tide and Ember, Strata and Gale — clash. A Spring thrown in on top of its opposite enters only by half, and the other half sinks into the land around as murk. Whatever went in first stays whole: the order you throw things in is part of the craft.

A Crucible holds sixty-four parts of currents. Past that it boils over: the excess steams off as murk from the fullest current, a drop at a time, until the distillate evens out. Steam and dark flakes over the rim always show — that is your sign to stop.
A comparator by the Crucible tells how full it is.

nodes.hint: What becomes of currents in the Crucible: which get along and which clash.

pages.t: Fluxsteel is the metal of flux instruments: the Conduit, the Confluence Heart, the Flux Coil, the Flux Reservoir, retorts, bands and fluxsteel tools and armor are made of it. It is iron steeped in distillate until the flux has soaked it through: darker than plain steel and heavier in the hand, with a thin vein of light glowing in its fracture.

Strata is in stone, Ember in coal, Lattice in diorite, quartz and Lattice crystals; Strata and Ember are neighbors and get along. The heat must be strong: iron melts only over lava. Throw the iron ingot in last.

kp: Слиток флюкс-стали Fluxsteel Ingot Слиток флюкс-стали Fluxsteel Ingot
nodes.hint: Steel steeped in flux: dark, with a vein of light inside. Read iron with the Loupe — and keep lava under the Crucible.

pages.t: The Crucible heals: tonics simmer in it over a gentle fire, and the first of them, the bloom tonic, closes wounds. Old herb women brewed such things in cauldrons without knowing they were brewing currents. The bloom tonic is Bloom, life itself, thinned with Tide.

Bloom is in bread, apples and eggs; Tide is in water and kelp. Throw the glass bottle in last. Keep the heat gentle: at a strong boil the tonic curdles and the bottle dissolves. Once drunk, the tonic mends wounds for twelve seconds.

kp: Цветочный отвар Bloom Tonic Цветочный отвар Bloom Tonic
nodes.hint: Not everything in the Crucible is metal and gems. Read a flower with the Loupe.

pages.t: Reforming gives plain materials you would otherwise have to go out for: clay from sand, string from wool, cobweb from string, a lava bucket from an empty bucket, and sea reforming gives prismarine, a sea lantern and a sponge without an ocean monument. The Crucible does not only dissolve: a thing thrown last into a brew of the right currents comes out as something else. Caustic Brine and the Murk Flask grew from the same craft.
Clay: sand soaked in three parts of Tide over a gentle heat comes out as four clay balls. Tide is in water and kelp.
String: white wool unpicked by a part of Bind and a part of Fang gives four strings; any heat will do.
Cobweb: string beaten together by three parts of Bind becomes a cobweb; any heat will do.
Lava: an empty bucket thrown into eight parts of Ember and two of Strata at a strong boil, over lava, floats up as a lava bucket — a Crucible over lava makes the lava for the next one.
Sea reforming: quartz washed in three parts of Tide and two of Prism over a gentle heat comes out as two prismarine shards. At a strong boil with Gleam the same quartz turns to opaline.
Crystals: a prismarine shard thrown into two parts of Tide and three of Gleam brightens into two prismarine crystals; any heat will do. Gleam is in glowstone dust.
Sea lantern: a glowstone block in eight parts of Tide, six of Prism and two of Gleam floats up as a sea lantern; any heat will do.
Sponge: a dried kelp block wrung out by two parts of Tide and four of Hollow at a strong boil, over lava, comes out as a dry sponge. Hollow is in tuff and in ender pearls.

nodes.hint: The Crucible makes one thing into another. Read sand with the Loupe.

pages.t: A Brimming Jug gives water on its own: by a river, a sea or a swamp it tops up cauldrons and Crucibles beside and below it and keeps the farmland around it moist — the wider, the more Tide there is in the place. A flower pot thrown into a brew of Tide and Halo comes out as a Brimming Jug. It draws not flux but the Tide of the place: in a desert or in dry mountains the jug is silent.

kp: Полный кувшин Brimming Jug Полный кувшин Brimming Jug
nodes.hint: A jug that draws the Tide of its place.

pages.t: An orb is light with no candle and no support, an Ember orb also heats a Crucible without fire, and any orb marks vessels. Glowstone dust is Gleam asleep in stone: thrown into a distillate where a single primal current has gathered, it curls around it into an orb of living flux. The orb hangs where it was placed and shines at full strength; you walk through it, and a touch takes it down whole.

Gather four parts of the orb's current and one part of Gleam, then throw the dust in last — two orbs come out. The dust gives the Gleam itself: the first pinch dissolves and leaves it in the distillate. Keep the heat gentle: at a strong boil the dust multiplies. If there is Halo in the brew, the dust gives a glint, not an orb.

Two orbs in one brew. If the dust fits two at once — say, the distillate holds both Strata and Ember — the orb whose current there is more of is born. With equal parts, the first in this row of runes: Tide, Strata, Ember, Gale, Lattice, Fray.
An ember orb is warm. Set it under a Crucible, and the Crucible will simmer over gentle heat without fire or smoke for as long as you like.

An orb marks vessels. Touch an empty, unbranded vessel with it, and the orb sinks into the bronze tag and burns the rune of its current there: the vessel will call that current along the siphons before a single part has reached it. A filled vessel is branded with flint and steel, by what is inside. To set an orb down beside a vessel, sneak.

kp: Сгусток Прилива Tide Orb Сгусток Жара Ember Orb Сгусток Жара Ember Orb
nodes.hint: Light that needs neither a candle nor a hook to hang from. Read glowstone dust with the Loupe.

pages.t: Bindwax locks a vessel: a sealed vessel neither gives nor takes, and a store of distillate will not run off through the siphons. Bind is the current of snares and ties, Root that of plants; brewed together on honeycomb, they give bindwax: soft, dark as honey, sticking to the fingers.
Bind hides in cobwebs, string and slime; Root in wood and wheat. Throw the honeycomb in last; any heat will do. One honeycomb yields two pieces of wax.

kp: Узовый воск Bindwax Узовый воск Bindwax
nodes.hint: Wax that holds tighter than resin. Read a honeycomb with the Loupe.

pages.t: Opaline need not be sought in the depths — it can be grown: a Crucible over lava turns quartz into opaline. Quartz is opaline that lacked the light: sink it in a distillate of Prism and Gleam, and turquoise and lilac begin to play inside it — the quartz remembers what it might have been.
Prism is in quartz, amethyst and gems; Gleam is in glowstone dust. Gems are hard, and quartz all the more: the Crucible must boil over lava. Throw the quartz in last.

kp: Opaline from Quartz Опалин из кварца
nodes.hint: The gem of the depths can be grown in the Crucible. Read quartz with the Loupe.

pages.t: The Crucible gives quickdust without shards: one redstone dust makes three pinches. Quickdust is all four Springs asleep in a pinch. Gather two parts each of Tide, Strata, Ember and Gale in the distillate, throw the redstone dust in last, and three pinches rise out of the Crucible.
